summary: For ages 11-12: pupils connect insect pollination (pollinators transferring pollen to the stigma so flowers can be fertilised and set fruit/seed) to human food security, learning that losing pollinators threatens the DIVERSITY and yield of food rather than all calories, because staple cereals (wheat, rice, maize) are wind-pollinated while many fruits, nuts and vegetables depend on insect pollination. Pupils reason about causes of decline (habitat loss, pesticides, disease) and mitigations (wildflower margins, hedgerows, reduced spraying), treating this as a specific, high-stakes case of interdependence. The central activity is a farm/landscape model that couples a pollinator population to crop yields; supporting activities add an in-role interview, a plate/market reveal scene, and a sorting/justification check, each with a distinct pedagogical purpose.
misconceptions: Thinking pollinator decline would starve us of all food, not realising wind-pollinated staple cereals are unaffected — it's diversity and yield at stake.
Believing pollination is the same as fertilisation, or that plants set fruit without pollen transfer.
Assuming only honeybees pollinate, overlooking wild bees, hoverflies, butterflies and other pollinators.
Thinking flowers exist to look pretty rather than being adaptations to attract specific pollinators for reproduction.

activities.title: Farm-and-pollinator landscape model: break and repair the dependency
steps: Tend a mixed landscape containing an apple orchard, oilseed rape, strawberry beds and a wheat field, alongside a pollinator (bee) population.

Apply a stressor — spray pesticide or clear hedgerows — and observe how the pollinator numbers fall and, crop by crop, the insect-pollinated plots set less fruit or seed so their harvests fall (sharply for apples; less for strawberries and oilseed rape, which can partly self-pollinate and benefit from, rather than wholly depend on, insects), while the wind-pollinated wheat keeps yielding.
Inspect a harvest/market-shelf readout and describe what changes: the shelf holds far fewer apples and strawberries and less rapeseed oil, but still holds bread.
State in writing whether pollinator loss threatens calories, variety, or both, using the wheat contrast as evidence.

Intervene by sowing wildflower margins, restoring hedgerows and cutting spraying, then observe over successive seasons whether pollinators and harvests recover, and explain which mitigation helped and why.
activities.insight: Pollinator decline reduces the variety in our diet and the yields of insect-pollinated crops rather than removing all calories, because insect-pollinated crops produce less (some far less) while wind-pollinated staples continue; this is a broken interdependence that can be mitigated, though recovery is gradual rather than instant.

activities.title: Interview a beekeeper, farmer or pollination ecologist
steps: Interview an in-role beekeeper, farmer or pollination ecologist about why pollinators — wild bees and other insects as well as managed honeybee colonies — are declining or under pressure, and what it means for the harvest.
Probe a concrete real case — for example almond orchards' heavy reliance on managed honeybees, or oilseed rape — to ground the dependency in a specific farming system.
Ask which mitigations actually work and press the persona to weigh trade-offs (e.g. cost of leaving field margins uncultivated vs. benefit to yields).
Summarise the persona's reasoning and decide which proposed solution the pupil would back, justifying the choice.
activities.insight: The decline-causes-consequences-solutions strand is a socio-scientific judgement: evidence and trade-offs, not just a single 'right' fix.

activities.title: What's on your plate: reveal insect- vs wind-pollinated foods
steps: Examine a plate or market scene and, for each food, reveal whether it needs or benefits from insect pollination, is wind-pollinated, or does not depend on pollination for the part we eat (e.g. potatoes, carrots, lettuce).
For an insect-pollinated food, identify a pollinator responsible (e.g. wild bees, honeybees, hoverflies, butterflies).
Drill down into one example to see a flower being pollinated, then state in a sentence what the pollinator did.
activities.insight: Much of the variety on a plate depends on specific pollinators, while staples like bread do not — making the dependency concrete before the modelling work.

activities.title: Sort crops and justify a mitigation
steps: Sort a set of crops into insect-pollinated vs wind-pollinated.
Answer a question on the likely consequences of pollinator decline for food supply.
Match each decline cause (habitat loss, pesticides, disease) to a plausible mitigation.
Choose a 'best mitigation' for a given scenario and write a one-sentence justification linking it to the cause.
activities.insight: Pupils can retrieve the crop categories and cause→mitigation links and justify a solution choice.

checkQuestion: Put this claim to the child: 'If bees disappeared we'd lose honey, but our food would be fine.' Ask: 'Is that right? Explain what bees actually do for crops like apples and almonds — and be precise about what pollination is and what it is not.'
checkAnswer: Not right. Bees and other insects POLLINATE many crops — they carry pollen between flowers so the plants can be fertilised and set fruit and seed. Apples, almonds and oilseed rape depend on this, so losing pollinators threatens food, not just honey. Pollination is the TRANSFER of pollen to the stigma; it is NOT fertilisation, which is the later joining of the pollen cell with the egg cell inside the ovule.
